title: From a maker’s engine order to a steamboat in service
question: Can a Boulton & Watt works record be joined to the engine that powered Fulton’s North River Steamboat and to a documented passenger voyage?
summary: Boulton & Watt’s invoice and dispatch correspondence match Fulton’s identification of the 1804 engine in his New York–Albany passenger boat. A signed passenger account records the first packet passage of 4–5 September 1807. The works code and the direct delivery and installation records remain open.
inputs: Maker and buying parties, including trading or forwarding names
Approximate order, dispatch and operating dates
Vessel names, registration jurisdiction and route
Machine specifications and markers distinguishing successive orders or refits

steps.title: Bound the vessel and its configuration
steps.action: Search port or customs registers for the vessel name and owner. Search each spelling or alias in a dated interval. Record the issuing office, enrollment or hull number, previous enrollment, dimensions and date of each rebuild. Use name changes and surrender or cancellation notes to identify the vessel at the proposed service date.
steps.result: The 14 May 1808 enrollment printed by Dickinson names the enlarged North River Steamboat of Clermont and cites the surrender of New York enrollment no. 973, issued 3 September 1807. The operator’s contemporary advertisement is headed The North River Steam Boat. Searches should include North River Steam Boat, North River Steamboat of Clermont and Fulton or Livingston. Clermont in the signed passenger account is a landing along the route. No. 973 belongs to the vessel enrollment.

steps.title: Identify the maker’s numbering system
steps.action: Open the maker’s production series and read its cataloguing notes on order numbers, shop codes, drawing numbers and reused sequences. Use the date range to choose the main volume and any overlapping small-engine or dispatch volumes. Search contemporary customer spellings, intermediaries, dimensions and places. Record the volume and folio, exact mark and adjacent fields. Match the mark in a second dated maker document before assigning it to the engine.
steps.result: Birmingham’s MS 3147/4 finding aid says Boulton & Watt added letter codes to orders, production and fitting books, packing and billing records from February 1803 and later repeated sequences. Engine Order Book No. 5, MS 3147/4/91, encloses the July 1804 order within its December 1802–October 1804 main sequence, with a second small-engines sequence. MS 3147/3/496 indexes Fulton’s letters, including two written as Robert Francis. Searches for Fulton, R. Fulton, Robert Francis, 24 inch and engine order book identified the relevant volume and correspondence. The item catalogue gives no Fulton folio and no engine code. The scanned September drawing names R. Fulton, but I could not verify the abbreviated shop notation as a code. The 1244a–c numbers in the correspondence calendar are drawing portfolio references.

steps.title: Follow the engine forward from order to delivery
steps.action: Read the signed authorization, specifications, invoice, packing list and dispatch letters in date order. Transcribe buyer, destination, carrier, dimensions and which parts were supplied. Follow each destination in the receiving port, yard or operator archive. Treat a works handover, forwarding instruction, loaded freight, port receipt and installation as separate milestones. Compare names, quantities, dates and any shared engine code at each handoff.
steps.result: The calendar records Fulton’s 28 July 1804 authorization. The cylinder and condenser drawing for R. Fulton is dated 13 September. The maker’s account of 17 January 1805 names Fulton, specifies a 24-inch bore and four-foot stroke, and lists Soho as the point of delivery. The dispatch letter of the same date describes packed goods awaiting carriage during frozen-canal conditions. The 21 February letter reports that Skey & Bird’s boats took the goods on 6 February for London. The surviving reproductions establish dispatch toward the London addressee. I found no transatlantic freight entry, signed receipt or contemporaneous installation handover in these reproductions.

steps.title: Trace the installed machine backward from the operator
steps.action: Search the operator’s engineering books, vessel accounts, repair records and dated letters for an explicit link to the maker’s order. Compare the configuration date, recipient and specs against the supplier record. Test the nearest competing earlier or later order and any rebuild. Inspect accession records and original drawings for later labels or retouched captions. Attribute shared-source transcriptions to the same underlying document.
steps.result: On 15 September 1810 Fulton told Boulton & Watt that their engine made for him in 1804, with a 24-inch cylinder and four-foot stroke, powered a New York–Albany passenger boat. The builder and recipient agree with the invoice. In the same letter Fulton asks for another engine, initially of 26 inches, with later changes in correspondence. This second order cannot identify the engine used in the 1807 voyage. The 1798 Livingston inquiry already mentions the earlier dimensions, so size alone is insufficient. U.S. National Museum staff examined drawing no. 180137 and identified the machinery layout as the remodeled North River vessel, flagging its later inscription. That drawing cannot establish the unmodified 1807 installation. Dickinson’s transcription and the correspondence calendar point to the same Fulton letter.

steps.title: Verify an actual duty or journey
steps.action: Use the operator’s notice to identify the date, location, fares and intended service. Search original local newspapers and the terminal’s arrival, clearance or passenger registers around the advertised date and across both termini. Identify the author, witnesses and any reprint lineage for each report. Look for a completed journey or recorded duty and match the vessel, route and operating purpose to the installation. Check trial runs, departures and advertisements separately.
steps.result: The 2 September 1807 American Citizen facsimile in New York State Library BOX 409 offers a 4 September departure from Paulas Hook ferry and a seven-dollar Albany fare. Its timings are advertised. In Wilson’s account in the Annals of Albany, a signed passenger statement dated at Albany on 5 September states the boat left New York on Friday and reached Albany the following morning on its first packet passage. Wilson identifies Friday as 4 September and signs the reported statement. The passengers provide an account independent of the builder and operators. Wilson says the Albany Register printed it on 8 September 1807. The New York State Library inventory identifies the Albany Register run with gaps, and the account was examined in its 1855 reprint. The August trial report and an October departure report refer to other passages. A fare offer and signatures do not establish an individual payment or a total passenger count.

decision: The producer’s 1805 invoice and the buyer’s 1810 letter support a supply relationship from Boulton & Watt’s 1804 Fulton order to the engine in his New York–Albany passenger boat. The independent passenger statement supports actual packet service on 4–5 September 1807. The identifier-level link remains unresolved because no dated works-code entry or receiving-side identifier was verified. The evidence supports a scoped supplier attribution on the existing boat service record.
reject_if: Reject an exact-engine join when the matching number belongs to another numbering system, was assigned after a rebuild, or was reused in a different period. Reject a join based only on common dimensions, a similar name or repeated copies of the same underlying document. Treat an itinerary or announcement as intent until there is evidence of observed service.
stop_when: Close an identifier-level join when a dated maker record and delivery or installation record identify the same machine in the same configuration and independent evidence attests the claimed duty. If the relevant folio or receiving record is unavailable, stop at the strongest supported intermediate join and record the repository, item reference and exact missing fields. Here that means the entry and code in MS 3147/4/91, a dated second code-bearing works record, and any freight or installation record that connects it to the New York vessel.
next: For the next pilot start with the surviving engine and locate the maker and installation documents for the original vessel. Use the accession number to find collection history, then seek the maker’s own identifier and check passenger or harbour evidence for the advertised duty.
